OPTIONS:
- Keep my hand out and wait for the brown-sleeved carter to answer (for: earning pennies while the room is looking at me)
- Ask Tom if he has an apron or towel that wants mending, and sew it in plain view for a halfpenny (for: showing off my work so the carters trust me)
* Sit down beside the brown-sleeved carter, thread my needle, and say I'll do the first stitch before he's even agreed (for: making it easy for him to say yes without losing face in front of his friends)
- Go up to bed with my three pennies and try the square in the morning (for: rest, and a fresh start at Ida's door and Bet's stall)

DO: I slide onto the settle beside the brown-sleeved carter with a rustle and thread my needle where everyone can see. "There now, sir, no one's made a fool of by a stitch. Give me the elbow and I'll show you what a quarter hour can do. If it's not to your liking, you've lost nothing but a little sitting." Then I hold my hand out for the sleeve, gently this time, and smile as if I'd every right to it.

JOURNAL: I've pushed hard from across the room and the room has gone quiet on me, so I'll come close and make it easy for him instead. One honest mend in front of the benches should bring the others, and I need those pennies for Ida's door and, one day, a ribbon.

OPTIONS:
- Keep my hand out to the brown-sleeved carter and press him a fourth time (for: getting my first penny of the night, though the room has gone quiet on me)
* Drop the sales patter, sit down on the bench among the carters and ask them for news of the flood and the ford, then mend the thin elbow for nothing as a sample (for: warming the room to me so the pennies follow, and not being ignored)
- Go to Tom and offer to tidy a frayed cloth or apron for him as thanks for his kindness (for: a friendly face and an audience of one, but no pennies)
- Go up to bed early and save my three pennies (for: rest, but I'd be a nobody tomorrow)
DO: I laugh and tuck my hand away. "Goodness, I've been talking at you like a fishwife with a fish, haven't I! Shove up, gentlemen, and tell me properly, what's this about the ford and Farmer Dunn's barley?" I sit down beside the brown-sleeved fellow, thread a needle while he talks, and say, "Your elbow's going to give in this very minute, so I'll mend it for nothing and you can judge my stitches for yourselves."
JOURNAL: Three tries at selling and they only stared, so I'll go at it another way: listen, let them talk, and let my needlework do the showing off. A free mend with the whole table watching ought to bring in paying sleeves, and then a ribbon is not far off.

OPTIONS:
- Keep my hand out and wait for the brown-sleeved carter to give me his arm, perhaps sweetening the offer again (for: earning a few pennies from the carters while they're looking at me)
- Turn to the nearest friendly face, ask Tom to spread word that I'm mending, and sit down by the fire with the needle case ready (for: letting custom come to me without pressing the carters, and resting after the day)
- Go west to Market Square tomorrow to knock on Ida Fenn's door and offer my needle to her trade (for: a steadier place to sew and a step toward fine things)
* Drop my hand with a laugh, pick out a different carter, and ask him kindly to show me a button or a hem that wants seeing to (for: getting someone to say yes after the quiet, without making the first one feel pushed)
DO: I laugh brightly and let my hand fall. "Goodness, I do believe I've frightened the poor man with my enthusiasm!" I turn to the carter at the end of the bench, whose coat has a button hanging by a thread. "You, sir, that button won't last the road to the next town. Let me have it back on in two minutes, and if you like it, a penny is all I ask."
JOURNAL: The quiet is long enough that pressing the brown sleeve again would only make me look desperate, so I'll try a smaller, easier mend with someone else. One yes will get the room moving, and I need the pennies for Ida's window tomorrow and perhaps a ribbon.

OPTIONS:
- Keep pressing the brown-sleeved carter, sweetening the offer until he holds out his arm (for: earning a few pennies tonight and drawing the other carters in)
- Go over to Tom and ask whether he'd let me mend the inn's linen or his own cuffs for a penny or two (for: a steady small earning from someone who's already been kind to me)
- Give up for tonight, thank the room warmly, and go to bed so I'm fresh to call at Ida Fenn's door in the morning (for: rest, and a better first impression on the draper whose trade I want)
* Turn to the next carter along, since the brown sleeve isn't biting, and admire something of his, a waistcoat or a buckle, before offering to mend (for: getting someone in the room to say yes by being noticed first)

DO: I let my hand drop gracefully and laugh as though I'd meant it. "Well, the brown sleeve is shy, goodness! Now you, sir, with the red neckcloth, that is a lovely bit of weaving, and that button on your coat is hanging by a single thread, look. Give it here and I'll have it fast in a trice, a halfpenny and no more." I hold out my palm and wait for him.

JOURNAL: The brown-sleeved carter won't be pushed, and a third go at him would only make me look desperate. A kind word on the red neckcloth and a real loose button to point at should get someone to say yes, and a halfpenny is little enough to risk. I'm working toward a few more pennies, a name in the room, and then Ida's door.

OPTIONS:
- Keep pressing the brown-sleeved carter, offering a cheaper first mend, to win the room's custom (for: earning pennies while everyone is watching)
- Turn to Tom and ask whether any of the carters have torn or loose things he's seen, and whether he'd mind me mending in his taproom (for: getting a friendly word to help the carters trust me and keeping Tom's goodwill)
- Sit down by the fire with the nearest carter, start in on his sleeve without waiting for an invitation, and chat about the flood (for: warming the room up instead of pushing, so someone offers an arm willingly)
* Pick up the thin brown sleeve myself by sitting beside the carter, and say lightly, "Never mind the price, sir, let me just show you what I can do with that elbow," then start threading my needle (for: breaking the stalemate by showing my work and getting someone to say something kind)
DO: I slide onto the bench beside the brown-sleeved carter and thread my needle with a flourish, saying, "Never mind the price for now, sir, let me just show you what I can do with that elbow. Goodness, such a lovely bit of wool, it deserves better than to go thin!" I hold out my hand again, gently this time, and wait for him to give me his arm.
JOURNAL: The room has gone quiet and nobody has moved, so more talk of price won't help; showing what my needle can do might. If he likes the elbow, the others will hold out their arms and I'll have pennies and a kind word to carry to Ida's door.

OPTIONS:
- Keep pressing the brown-sleeved carter with my offer, maybe sweeten it further (for: earning pennies while the room is watching)
- Turn to Tom and ask whether he knows anyone with a torn hem or a coat to freshen, and offer to mend for the house at a fair price (for: a steadier bit of work and a friend in the innkeeper)
- Give the carters a moment, sit down with my needle case and mend my own sleeve in plain view, so they can see my stitching (for: showing my skill without pushing, and being looked at)
- Call it a night, go up to my paid bed, and be at Ida Fenn's window fresh in the morning (for: rest and a better start tomorrow)
* Sit down at the end of the long table and start mending a small rip in my own cuff in plain view, chatting brightly, so they can see my stitches (for: showing my skill without pushing, and being looked at)
DO: I give a little laugh and perch myself at the end of the long table, drawing out a needle and thread. "Well, if nobody's brave enough to go first, I shall simply mend my own cuff and let you watch, gentlemen. Goodness, look how neat that is going to be!" I start stitching, quick and bright, and glance up now and then to see who's peering.
JOURNAL: Pressing a third time felt like begging, and I'd rather be watched than turned down. If they see my stitches are fine, one of them will hold out an arm on his own, and I'll have pennies toward Ida's door and a ribbon.

OPTIONS:
- Ask Kit, who's the miller's lad, about the ford and the far bank, what the water does and where it's shallowest (for: learning how to string a guide line across the ford)
- Talk to Jory and Hobb about the new timbers and whether the bridge can be mended before the rain (for: helping get Dunn's barley across)
- Walk down to the ford stakes and look closely at the water and the banks, maybe testing the depth with a stick (for: finding out how the ford really runs and where a line could be anchored)
* Go to Kit first and ask what he's seen of the river and the ford, and whether he saw anything of the wage box or the tinker (for: both the ford and the wages mystery, from someone who lives by the mill)
DO: My dear colleague Kit! Fascinating spot you've got, fishing under the piers. Hypothesis: you know this river better than anyone in town. Where's the ford shallowest, and where does the current bite hardest? And did you see anything wash by the night of the flood, a box, a handcart, a tinker? I've three pennies and I'll make it worth your while.
JOURNAL: Kit lives by the water and can tell me more than the market gossip about the ford and the lost box. I'm working toward a guide line across the ford for Dunn's barley and toward finding Agnes's wages.

OPTIONS:

* Go east to the Wheatsheaf and look for Agnes there (for: finding the reeve to be paid for the beams and to give her Kit's word about the green box)
DO: I nod to Bet. "Fair enough. Obliged." Then I stop, and say, "No. Here's a penny for your trouble," and set it on her stall. I go east to the Wheatsheaf, to look for Agnes, counting my steps under my breath.
JOURNAL: Wage is owed and Kit's word is Agnes's by right, so I go on looking for her. I'd not take Bet's help for nothing, so I pay her a penny rather than owe her thanks. I'm working toward a door that locks and owing nobody.

* Ask Sam the price of a long iron hook and what he'd want for it, then bargain (for: the box, the six pennies and my name on the fetching)

JOURNAL: The hook is the safest way to reach the box, and the box means six pennies and my name as the one who fixed it. I ask the price first, as ever, and sleep at the Wheatsheaf once it's ordered.
